title: Island topography + urbanism
oneLiner: An island's terrain, roads and drainage, rebuilt as native Revit elements.
problem: Planners and architects on a live project needed the island's earthworks and urbanism in Revit, beyond what native terrain tools handle well.
approach: Terrain built in Civil 3D and Rhino, then brought into Revit as native topography, floors, drainage and railings through Rhino.Inside and Grasshopper.
result: One live Revit model with terrain, roads, paving and urban systems, and total earthworks volume calculated in Grasshopper.
coordination: [Pending: your role, the team, and how the planners' design changes reached the model.]

hero.alt: The same part of the island three times: Rhino BREP surfaces, native Revit topography, native Revit floors
hero.caption: Rhino BREP surfaces, then native Revit topography, then native Revit floors.

sections.heading: One terrain to build on
sections.text: The topography of the whole island was built at the start of the project, combining Civil 3D and Rhino. Working alongside the urban planners and architects, every design decision after that (roads, paving, urban furniture, energy systems) was placed on top of it.

figures.alt: Exploded axonometric of the island terrain in layers, with a colour map of the earthworks volume
figures.caption: The terrain in layers, with the total earthworks volume calculated in Grasshopper.

sections.heading: From mesh to native Revit
sections.text: A base mesh became editable Rhino surfaces, then native Revit elements: topography, floors adapted to the terrain, and linear elements like drainage and railings. Each step was a Grasshopper script through Rhino.Inside, so changes could be pushed through again.

figures.alt: Diagram: base topography mesh, Civil 3D and Rhino, editable Rhino BREP topography, then native Revit topography, floors and linear elements

title: Stadium façade: BIM to fabrication
oneLiner: One master model that writes every fabrication file.
problem: The client needed a precise Revit model of a stadium's façade structure, and then fabrication models for every piece, normally built in separate software.
approach: I automated both steps with Rhino.Inside Revit and Grasshopper: a full BIM model for clash detection, and scripts that read Revit parameters to export fabrication STP files.
result: When the Revit model changed, the fabrication files updated with it, and no separate fabrication software was needed.
coordination: [Pending: your role, the team and external parties, and how the work was run.]

hero.alt: Exploded axonometric of the façade substructure layers, next to one fabrication-ready substructure piece with its connection details
hero.caption: From the simplified façade substructure to a fabrication-ready piece.

sections.heading: One model, two jobs
sections.text: It started as advisory on a precise Revit model of the façade structure, and grew into two tasks: a full BIM model for clash detection, within the system and against other disciplines like the main stadium structure, and fabrication models that read their data from that base model.

figures.alt: Workflow from the base stadium grids through Rhino.Inside Revit to substructure placement, clash detection and automatic fabrication export

sections.heading: Automated end to end
sections.text: Every step ran through Rhino.Inside Revit and Grasshopper, from the stadium grids to the eaves and the substructure. When fabrication issues came up, the Revit model changed and the export scripts rebuilt the STP files, so every fabrication file stayed fed by the one model.

title: Sensi
oneLiner: A copilot that scores how each room will feel, across six senses.
problem: Floor plans get checked for structure, cost and energy, but not for how each room will feel to the person living in it.
approach: It learns a user's sensory profile, scores every room with fixed rules, and lets them edit the plan in plain language. The LLM routes and explains; it never sets the score.
result: Trade-offs like 'bigger window, more noise, colder room' become visible across a whole plan, re-scored live on every edit.
coordination: Led by Emilie El Chidiac. I built the back end and front end and refined the LLM layer.
team: Emilie El Chidiac, Lakzhmy Mari Zaro, Charles Abi Chahine and me.

hero.alt: Galaxy view: rooms, senses and design levers as one glowing network
hero.caption: The galaxy view: rooms, senses and the design levers behind them, as one map.

sections.heading: A missing layer
sections.text: We model structure, cost, energy and code, but not how a room will feel. Sensi reads a floor plan and scores each room across six senses (thermal, visual, acoustic, spatial, olfactory and tactile) for one specific person.

figures.alt: Exploded axonometric: floor plan, structure, cost and energy layers, with the sensory layer on top
figures.caption: The sensory layer: personal, honest, coupled.

sections.heading: The ripple
sections.text: The senses pull on each other. A bigger window brings in daylight, but the glass is also a thinner sound barrier and leaks heat. Sensi shows the whole chain of consequences, not just the upgrade you see.

figures.alt: Ripple diagram: a bigger window gives visual +0.15, acoustic −0.10 and thermal −0.08
figures.caption: The upgrade you see, and the costs you don’t.

sections.heading: Same plan, two people
sections.text: Comfort isn't universal. A child who minds noise and a grandmother who minds the cold flag different rooms in the same plan, so Sensi starts by learning who it's scoring for.

figures.alt: Split floor plan: the child's lens flags the loud living room, the grandmother's lens the cold bedroom
figures.caption: The same rooms, lit by who is standing in them.

sections.heading: Act 1: Onboard
sections.text: A few questions, then a moodboard. Every image someone keeps nudges the weights of the six senses, which compile into a persona drawn as a petal rose. Picking images says more than rating tactile comfort from 1 to 5.

figures.alt: Screen recording of the moodboard rounds and the persona petal rose
figures.caption: Moodboard rounds, then the persona.

sections.heading: Levers and coupling
sections.text: Six design levers (glazing, orientation, ventilation, volume, materials and adjacency) each pull on one or more senses. A room's score is half mean, half worst: the sense that's wrong is the one you notice.

figures.alt: Coupling diagram linking six design levers to six senses, coded as helps, harms or trade-off
figures.caption: Which levers help, harm or trade off each sense.

sections.heading: Act 2: Shape
sections.text: You talk to the plan in plain language. A fast model routes the request, a heavier one explains or plans the edit, and the room is re-scored. The scoring itself is deterministic, so every change can be traced, and every edit is kept as a checkpoint.

figures.alt: Flow diagram of the Shape agent: understand, edit and see anew
Screen recording of a kitchen being scored and its conflicts listed
figures.caption: Scoring a room and finding its conflicts.

figures.alt: Screen recording of edits applied to the plan and kept as checkpoints
figures.caption: Edits, re-scored and kept as checkpoints.

sections.heading: Act 3: Report
sections.text: The final scores write a prompt, and a vision model renders each room. Only clearly good or bad senses add a phrase, so the render shows what actually changed.

figures.alt: Scores becoming a prompt, then a before and after render of a kitchen
Screen recording comparing before and after renders of a room
figures.caption: Same room, same angle: only the change moves.

sections.heading: What stays open
sections.text: The ripple and the veto did reprioritise rooms. Still open: there's no ground-truth data to prove the scores, and a confident number can quietly decide for the designer instead of helping them decide.

figures.alt: Summary: what holds and what stays open

title: Model data, made visible
kind: MaCAD, IAAC, extended with my own APS work
oneLiner: Performance data placed inside the model as geometry, then checked automatically in the cloud.
problem: Three studio teams produced geometry, but no one owned the data, so performance KPIs stayed in spreadsheets.
approach: We set naming and parameter standards, then used Rhino.Inside Revit to place KPI families and fill shared parameters automatically. I'm now checking that standard on the AEC Data Model.
result: Thermal, acoustic and air-quality KPIs readable in the model, with filters, sheets and IFC export.
coordination: I worked at the planning level: the initial standards and the order of work across teams, while my teammates focused on execution and code. The Forma extension is my own work.
team: Lakzhmy Mari Zaro, Emilie El Chidiac and me, as the studio's data team.

hero.alt: Three tower models coloured by thermal, acoustic and air-quality KPIs
hero.caption: Three KPIs, read as geometry in the model.

sections.heading: The data team
sections.text: Hyperbuilding 01 was one of three linked megastructures for Santiago de Chile, designed to filter air and water. Other teams worked on structure, façade and program. We were the coordination layer: naming conventions, information structure, the timing of decisions, and turning design into usable data.

figures.alt: The data team’s four roles and their outputs, from weekly timeline to internal updates

sections.heading: A control room
sections.text: A web app that pulls the project's information into one place: a KPI dashboard, a status diagram, a health check, and a timeline of each team's milestones.

figures.alt: Control room web app: KPI dashboard, status diagram, health check and timeline

sections.heading: Making data spatial
sections.text: If the data team doesn't draw geometry, how does its work show up in the model? Three parametric Revit families turn KPIs into elements: a thermal panel, a noise orbit and a pollutant sphere.

sections.heading: The workflow
sections.text: Grasshopper reads positions from the shared Speckle model. Rhino.Inside Revit sets the levels, places the families and fills their shared parameters. Views, sheets and filters with gradient overrides follow, ready for RVT, IFC or PDF.

sections.heading: The result
sections.text: Each KPI is readable in the model itself: boxes coloured by thermal compliance, noise orbits on every level, and pollutant spheres where purification demand is highest.

sections.heading: A dashboard on the AEC Data Model
sections.text: After the studio, I took the naming and parameter standard further on my own: a dashboard with a Python back end and a Vue front end, built on Autodesk Platform Services. It reads the Revit model in the cloud and shows, version by version, how much of each KPI family meets the standard.

figures.alt: Model Data Quality dashboard: one card per KPI family with its compliance percentage, and a chart of compliance per version
figures.caption: Overview: each KPI family and how it evolved across eight versions.

sections.heading: How it checks
sections.text: You sign in with your Autodesk account and pick the model. The app asks the AEC Data Model API for each family's elements, only the KPI parameters, for any version. Every value is checked against a rules file (format, allowed list, range, unique) and ends up OK, breaking the standard, or missing.

figures.alt: Flow diagram: Autodesk sign-in, AEC Data Model API, then per element: has a value, follows the rules, ending in OK, breaks standard or missing

sections.heading: What to fix
sections.text: The evolution shows when each parameter reached the standard. For anything still failing, the dashboard lists the Revit element IDs and the problem, so whoever owns the model can find and fix them directly.

figures.alt: Chart of the share of elements meeting the standard per parameter across versions v1 to v8
figures.caption: Per parameter, per version.

figures.alt: Table of KPI_NoiseOrbit elements to fix, with Revit element IDs, values and problems
figures.caption: Elements to fix, by Revit ID.

title: Computational bucketing
oneLiner: Every element coloured by its value, on every new model version.
problem: Checking how a property spreads across a model meant clicking through elements one by one, and left out anyone without a Speckle account.
approach: A Speckle Automate function groups elements by a chosen property and feeds a web viewer coloured by range.
result: A 25–30 minute model review now takes under three minutes.
coordination: [Pending: your role in the team of three.]
team: Lakzhmy Mari Zaro, Emilie El Chidiac and me.

hero.alt: Hyperbuilding model recoloured bucket by bucket, from red to blue
hero.caption: The model, bucket by bucket.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: On every new model version, the function flattens the object tree, reads a chosen numeric property and groups elements into range buckets. Each bucket is published as a sub-model, together with a manifest and a visualisation model that the website reads.

figures.alt: Diagram of the Automate function: inputs, function steps and outputs feeding the website viewer

sections.heading: How many buckets
sections.text: Different properties spread differently, so the bucket count is a choice: Scott's rule, square root, Sturges' rule, or a manual number when domain knowledge matters more than statistics.

figures.alt: The four bucketing methods: Scott's rule, square root, Sturges' rule and manual input

sections.heading: For the reviewer
sections.text: Set up the automation once and pick a property. The website shows the model coloured by range, with no Speckle account needed, and stays current with every version.
